chromeos: turn on USE=forced-sandbox for mawk & sed We currently always turn this on for mawk via a bashrc, so this doesn't change behavior there. It just makes it easier to sync with Gentoo and drop our local patches (in the future). For sed, this is new behavior. We're disabling support for the e/r/w commands because (1) we don't care about them and have no known legit users and (2) they needlessly expose random shell scripts to attacks. common-mk: Don't include sources in inputs for generating dbus bindings. Tip-of-tree GYP doesn't allow ${source} to end up in the inputs list. generate-dbus-adaptors.gypi and generate-dbus-proxies.gypi supply the sources as inputs, which are translated into ${source} at ninja generation time, causing assert failures with ToT GYP. Providing these as inputs does not appear to be necessary, and other generator .gypi files do not, so remove them to allow ToT GYP to be used. CHROMIUM: tpm: cr50_spi: set flow control timeout to timeout A It is possible that the TPM can become unresponsive for longer than the currently used flow control timeout in cr50_spi driver. The spec doesn't define the max time that the TPM can be unresponsive. However, for aborting commands the timeout is set at Timeout A. Use the same timeout for flow control. ftdiuart: Put in an explicit delay for sending a break Recently after switching to a new desktop, Linux version, and reogranizing my USB devices (not sure which of the three was important), I found that I could no longer manage to send a break through servo to cause a SYSRQ on Linux. Although I didn't scope the signal, I postulated that perhaps the break signal was not being held long enough. After all, the API to libftdi just allows you to start asserting a break and then stop. It doesn't appear to have any sort of timing built in. Sure enough, adding a usleep() between asserting the break and deasserting it fixed my problem. From some quick searching, it appears that you're supposed to hold the break state for "longer than one frame time". That's pretty easy to calculate since a frame is made up of: - 1 start bit - 7 or 8 data bits - 0 or 1 parity bits - 1, 1.5, or 2 stop bits ...or, at most 12 bits. Apparently there are separate concepts for "short break" and "long break" but we don't really have the ability to get such precise timing so we'll just make sure that we at least qualify for some type of break and call it a day. BUG=None TEST=Type "<enter>`zg" and enter kgdb Change-Id: I40376afe6f466ff8112cfc6276a29fcf2f8f8960 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/962672 Commit-Ready: Douglas Anderson <dianders@chromium.org> Tested-by: Douglas Anderson <dianders@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Todd Broch <tbroch@chromium.org>
